transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Malhotra (Velora - ML Eng), Ethan Cole (Velora - CTO), Sara Kim (Velora - PM)
---
Summary (auto): weekly POC sync, benchmark review (latency/throughput) vs baseline provider; tuning suggestions; next steps documented.
---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call and then we can jump into the benchmark slide deck, um, hope you all had a good week
[00:08] Priya: yep thanks, all good, excited to see the numbers today
[00:12] Ethan: same here, we've been burning through the baseline results so curious how Redwood stacked up
[00:20] Liam: cool, i'll share my screen, just a heads up some of the labels in the CSV got munged so i put a note in the sheet about mapping columns, the raw logs are slightly different naming for kv cache entries
[00:35] Sara: ok great, that mapping will help, we ran the baseline with the vendor default config, no quant, no kv warm up
[00:45] Liam: yeah so first slide: p50/p95/p99 across the standard chat prompt set (avg seq length ~280 tokens). Baseline provider p95 ~320 ms, p99 ~470 ms. Redwood (hosted w/ tuning) p95 ~130 ms, p99 ~210 ms. numbers are median across 5 runs
[01:05] Priya: those are big diffs, is that with batching? what batch sizes were used?
[01:12] Liam: good question — baseline used static batching of 8 in their managed endpoint. we used dynamic batching + continuous batching, average eff batch ~10 because of request arrival patterns. we also enabled 4-bit quantization on the model variant we served (we tested q4_0 and q4_km) and the q4_km had slightly better perf with negligible quality change on the eval set
[01:35] Priya: hm transcription note — sometimes the q4 km showed slight hallucination on the long context, did you see that?
[01:42] Liam: we saw the eval scoring change by ~0.7% on the rouge-like metric for long-form contexts; for chat-turns it's within noise. we flagged the prompt set examples that regressed and put them in the spreadsheet
[01:58] Ethan: throughput numbers? tokens/sec or reqs/sec? we need to map to our SLOs, which are 200 qps peak, p95 latency <250ms
[02:06] Liam: throughput: baseline measured ~1.2k tokens/sec under the test profile, Redwood ~1.9k tokens/sec. in reqs/sec terms that maps roughly to baseline 85 rps and Redwood 130 rps for the workload. p95 latency for Redwood stayed under 160ms for the 95% traffic profile we've modeled
[02:30] Sara: so it meets our p95 target, nice. what's the cost delta?
[02:34] Maya: quick note on cost — rough ballpark from the benchmark runs: per-token inference cost on baseline provider was about 35% higher. couple caveats: baseline runs didn't use our batch/caching knobs, and their pricing model includes a per-request surcharge for small requests which made some of the short-turn costs worse
[02:54] Priya: can you say more about caching? we didn't enable any prefix cache on the baseline so i want to be careful comparing apples to apples
[03:02] Liam: absolutely — we enabled prefix/KV caching where appropriate. because many calls have repeated system prompts and user preamble, the KV cache stops recomputing attention for the prefix so effective token compute dropped, that helped latency a lot on mid-long sequences
[03:20] Priya: i remember seeing a note about 'K V cash' in the transcript last week — just making sure the logs show key-value not cash :)
[03:26] Liam: yep — transcription funnies aside, raw server logs use kv_cache.* metric names, but the exported CSV had the column kv_cache_hits spelled 'k v cache hits' once for one run, so mapping required
[03:40] Ethan: any variability or outliers? our infra folks are wary of p99 spikes when sequences hit 2k tokens
[03:48] Liam: good call. we did a targeted test on 2k sequences — baseline p99 shot up to ~1.2s, Redwood p99 to ~430ms — so still better but definitely increases. main mitigation is to use model variants trimmed for long context or to shard long requests and stream
[04:08] Priya: what about cold-starts or KV cold misses?
[04:12] Liam: cold starts exist, we observed first-request latency of about 1.8s in the worst case on both providers if no warm pool existed. but Redwood offers an optional warm pool and keep-alive settings; with a small warm pool the cold-start tail goes away for our traffic shape
[04:30] Sara: can you walk us through the tuning knobs you changed?
[04:33] Liam: sure — list is: q4_km quantization, dynamic continuous batching, prefix/KV caching, kernel selection optimization (we pinned kernels for the MHA path for sequence lengths 128-512), and adjusted autoscale cooldowns (faster scale up, buffered scale down). also turned on token-streaming with chunked responses for end-user perceived latency
[04:58] Priya: did you try changing temperature/beam settings? those affect compute slightly
[05:02] Liam: we kept sampling params constant to isolate perf; lower temperature doesn't change compute, beam search would increase compute but our use case uses sampling so not relevant
[05:12] Ethan: can you share the raw profiler traces? our infra wants to see GPU utilization and memory patterns
[05:18] Liam: yes that's in the raw logs i mentioned — GPU util graphs, kernel-time breakdowns, mem alloc patterns, and per-step latencies — i'll attach those to the sheet. note: profiler files are large, i'll put a pointer to an S3 bucket link in the email
[05:34] Maya: let's also call out the security/compliance ask — Ethan you mentioned wanting KMS/HSM and audit logs for the POC?
[05:41] Ethan: yes, we need to validate key management for production. for POC we can use Redwood-managed keys, but for enterprise we will likely require customer KMS integration and audit logs to match our SOC 2 scope
[05:55] Maya: noted. Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integration and audit log forwarding; i'll include the security brief and SOC 2 cert copy in the artifacts we share
[06:06] Priya: what's the next step on the soak test — duration and load profile?
[06:10] Liam: recommended: 24h soak at a mixed traffic profile: 50% short-turn chats (~30 tokens), 40% mid (~200 tokens), 10% long (~1500-2k tokens). ramp to 70% of expected peak for the first 4 hours then hold, observe autoscale behavior and p99 tails
[06:28] Priya: ok we'll run that in staging. do you want us to use the Redwood hosted instance or spin up a Private trial?
[06:33] Maya: for soak i'd recommend Redwood hosted to get rapid results; if you want to validate VPC/KMS flows we can run a limited Private deployment afterwards — that'll be part of the Dedicated trial planning
[06:44] Ethan: pricing question — if we move to Dedicated, what are the expected commit levels? we have a seasonal peak and don't want to overcommit
[06:52] Maya: typical Dedicated is monthly reserve with burst to shared capacity; we can propose a baseline commit that hits your 75% 90th-percentile usage and allow burst. I'll draft a few tiers in the proposal. also note that Dedicated materially lowers per-token cost relative to hosted metered usage in many of our customers
[07:10] Sara: any concerns about model quality between quantized variants and the baseline?
[07:13] Liam: quality-wise, on our eval prompt set, q4_km had negligible regressions (mostly on long-form factual recall), we recommend running your critical prompt set through our eval harness — we can run a focused regressions check and return a short report
[07:30] Priya: please do that, we'll upload a canonical prompt set to the shared drive
[07:33] Maya: perfect — we'll run the eval and annotate any prompts that regress and propose mitigation (bump to q8 or use full-fp32 for those cases)
[07:46] Liam: small note: one test run had a mislabeled header so a few latency datapoints looked like outliers; we've reprocessed and the sheet reflects corrected numbers
[07:56] Ethan: thanks. can you also include cost modeling for 6/12/24 month commits so we can present to finance
[08:02] Maya: yes i'll include tiered pricing and sensitivity to usage in the proposal
[08:08] Sara: any competitive intel to call out? we mentioned CloudModelCo and VendorX earlier — did they present materially different numbers?
[08:15] Liam: CloudModelCo had comparable throughput on small sequences when they used aggressive batching, but their p99 on long sequences was worse and they lacked prefix caching so repeated prompts cost us more; VendorX had lower latency on tiny inputs but cost per token was higher once you normalize for quality
[08:36] Priya: ok good to know. any other risks?
[08:40] Liam: main risk is long-context quality with the quantized variant; mitigation is to use hybrid config where long-form prompts use a higher-precision variant. ops risk is autoscale tuning but we can share recommended policies and run a warm-up test
[08:55] Maya: let's capture action items — Liam will share the raw logs and full benchmark sheet by Friday; Priya will run the soak test and send results back by next Friday; Maya will share Dedicated trial proposal and security docs
[09:09] Priya: yup we'll do that
[09:12] Ethan: sounds good, thanks everyone
[09:15] Maya: thanks all, i'll follow up with links and scheduling for the Dedicated planning call
